prompt: Three independent voters are each right 80% of the time. What is the probability that their majority is right? Give it as a decimal.
hint: All three right, plus exactly two right.

prompt: Three independent voters are each right 40% of the time. How does their majority compare with one of them?
hint: Work out the same sum at 0.4.

choices.text: Better, as with any vote
choices.why: The gain only appears above one half.

choices.text: Exactly the same
choices.why: That would need the three to make the same mistakes.

choices.text: Worse: 0.352 against 0.4
choices.why: Right: a majority of voters who are usually wrong is wrong more reliably.

choices.text: It cannot be computed without knowing which voter is the best of the three
choices.why: All three have the same accuracy here; the sum needs nothing else.

prompt: The 0.896 for three voters at 80% depends on one assumption. Which?
hint: It is what lets you multiply the error rates.

choices.text: That the voters are prompts rather than models
choices.why: The arithmetic does not care what a voter is.

choices.text: That one voter's mistakes make no other's more likely
choices.why: Right: independence, which is what lets 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04.

choices.text: That ties are settled by the first voter
choices.why: With two labels and three voters there is no tie to settle.

choices.text: That every voter runs at temperature 0
choices.why: Temperature is not in the sum.

prompt: Three independent voters are each right 70% of the time. What is the probability that their majority is right? Give it as a decimal.
hint: 0.7 cubed, plus three times 0.7 squared times 0.3.

prompt: Three voters at 80% make exactly the same mistakes on exactly the same messages. How often is their majority right?
hint: When one is wrong, so are the others.

choices.text: 80% of the time, the same as any one of them
choices.why: Right: three copies of one voter are one voter.

choices.text: 89.6% of the time
choices.why: That needs independent mistakes.

choices.text: Never
choices.why: They are right together 80% of the time.

choices.text: 51.2% of the time, since all three must be right together
choices.why: When their mistakes coincide, being right together is the same 80%.

prompt: How many of the seventy cases did the majority of `v3-examples`, `v4-only-json` and `v6-escaped` get right?
`v3-examples` gets 54 of 70 right and the other two 45 each. Why does their majority get only 49?

choices.text: Three voters can never beat the best of them
choices.why: With independent mistakes they can; here they share them.

choices.text: The prompts were run at different temperatures
choices.why: All three ran at 0.

choices.text: The two weaker prompts outvote the strong one where they agree
choices.why: Right: five cases lost that way, and three more to ties.

choices.text: `vote.py` counts every reply that does not parse as wrong
choices.why: A reply that does not parse casts no ballot; that saved `t38`.

prompt: In the `uniq -c` count, how many cases were wrong under all three prompts?
Ten cases were wrong under exactly one of the three prompts. What did the vote do with them?

choices.text: Fixed all ten
choices.why: Right: the other two outvoted it.

choices.text: Fixed half of them
choices.why: Two right ballots beat one wrong one every time.

choices.text: Nothing, since they were already wrong
choices.why: Only one prompt had them wrong.

choices.text: Turned them into ties
choices.why: A tie needs the ballots split evenly.

prompt: In `vote.py`, a reply that does not parse casts no ___, and the other replies decide the case.
hint: What a voter puts in the box.

prompt: Independent voters this accurate would all be wrong on about two cases in seventy. These three were wrong together on twelve. What does that say?

choices.text: The arithmetic of the first section is wrong
choices.why: The arithmetic assumed independence, and that is what failed.

choices.text: Twelve is within chance of two
choices.why: Not at seventy cases.

choices.text: The holdout labels are wrong
choices.why: Nothing points there.

choices.text: Their mistakes are not independent
choices.why: Right: one model, the same blind spots.

prompt: Five samples per message at temperature 0.8, voted. How many of the seventy did the vote get right?
The vote of five samples got one message more than `v6-escaped` at temperature 0. Which one, and why?

choices.text: `h17`, where three samples found the right label
choices.why: Three samples of `h17` were wrong, and so was the vote.

choices.text: `t38`, whose reply at 0 is cut at an apostrophe
choices.why: Right: the samples wrote around the bug, F-0001.

choices.text: `t12`, a close call between two labels
choices.why: `t12` was right at 0 already.

choices.text: None; the extra one was a tie broken in its favour
choices.why: There were no ties among the samples.

prompt: A report says the vote of five samples at 0.8 beat a single sample at 0.8. What is wrong with the comparison?

choices.text: Temperature 0.8 is too high to sample at
choices.why: The comparison is the flaw, not the setting.

choices.text: Samples should be compared in tokens, not answers
choices.why: Answers are the point.

choices.text: It is measured against one of its own members
choices.why: Right: compare with the best single call, here 54.

choices.text: Five samples are too few to vote with
choices.why: The count is not the flaw.

prompt: Wang and others (2022) reported gains from self-consistency. What kind of task were they on, and why does that matter here?
hint: How many ways to the answer?

choices.text: Reasoning with many paths to one answer; a label has one path
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Classification, the same as here; the gain should carry over
choices.why: They sampled chains of reasoning.

choices.text: Translation, where variety is the point of sampling
choices.why: Arithmetic and commonsense questions.

choices.text: Short answers, where samples rarely differ
choices.why: Their samples were long chains.

prompt: How does `vote.py` count a case whose ballots tie?

choices.text: It takes the first ballot
choices.why: It breaks no ties.

choices.text: It drops the case from the total
choices.why: The total stays seventy.

choices.text: As right, if one of the tied labels is right
choices.why: It needs a single winner.

choices.text: As wrong
choices.why: Right: a tie is not a decision.

prompt: Per million messages, the three members cost 120,690, 80,083 and 87,797 cents. How many times the cost of `v3-examples` alone is the ensemble? One decimal place.
A provider runs an ensemble's calls at the same time. What is the wait for an answer?

choices.text: The fastest member's time
choices.why: The answer needs every ballot.

choices.text: The slowest member's time
choices.why: Right, and the bill is still all of them.

choices.text: The mean of the members' times
choices.why: The vote waits for the last ballot.

choices.text: The sum of every member's time
choices.why: That is when they run one after another, as `pl` does.

prompt: Which of these make an ensemble more likely to be worth what it costs? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A wrong answer is expensive
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Each call is cheap
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The members make different mistakes
choices.why: Yes: otherwise the vote cannot outvote them.

choices.text: The members are rewordings of one prompt
choices.why: Rewordings share the model's mistakes.
